children.value: matrix for every comparison. A Gabor filter bank convolves the image with a dozen large kernels. This section collects what the main text leaves out: how to compute moments in a single pass, how to replace the quadratic distance with a Euclidean one, two further texture features, namely gradient moments and Laws’ texture energy, and how Gabor filters work in Fourier space. Each subsection starts with a short reminder of the definition it builds on.

In the example, the four terms of the fourth moment are tens of millions, but the result is 445,000. Most of the value cancels, and rounding errors in the accumulated sums survive the subtraction. On the Matterhorn photo of

(1,091,840 pixels, mean lightness 60.9), a simple loop that accumulates the four sums in 32-bit floating point gives a variance that is 0.39% too low and a kurtosis that is 3.2% too high. Three remedies help. Accumulate in 64-bit floating point: the relative errors then stay below

. Subtract a rough estimate of the mean before accumulating, since the standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis, and covariance do not change when all values shift: subtracting 85, the mean of the first ten rows, reduces the 32-bit errors below 0.05%. Or use update formulas that keep running central moments instead of raw sums; they are numerically stable and can also merge partial results computed in parallel (see Pébay in the Further Reading).

children.value: Four moments for each quantity and one covariance give nine values that describe the gradient distribution. The mean magnitude measures how much edge energy the image contains. Its skewness is large when most of the image is flat and a few strong edges stand out. The moments of the direction show whether edges prefer certain directions. All nine values can be computed in one pass with the formulas of the previous subsection.

children.value: its aspect ratio. A filter bank combines several directions and scales, and the moments of the filtered images form the texture feature. This subsection shows how the filtering is computed in Fourier space and what the filters look like there.
The convolution theorem states that a convolution in image space becomes a pointwise multiplication in Fourier space:

children.html: I∗g=F−1(F(I)⋅F(g))I * g = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\bigl(\mathcal{F}(I) \cdot \mathcal{F}(g)\bigr)I∗g=F−1(F(I)⋅F(g))

children.value: shows the resulting pipeline. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) turns the grayscale image into a complex array with a real and an imaginary component. We multiply this array element by element with the Fourier transform of the Gabor filter, and the inverse FFT returns the filtered image. The filtered image is complex as well; its magnitude measures how strongly the selected frequency and direction are present at each pixel. For a bank of filters, the forward FFT of the image is computed only once and shared by all filters.

A straight, high-contrast edge concentrates its energy along a line through the center of the spectrum, perpendicular to the edge. In the windsurfer photo of
, the mast against the white foam creates such a spike. The three filters whose blobs lie on this spike show the mast; the filter with a different direction misses it.

applies four filters with the same directions and scales to a mountain photo. The spectrum at the bottom left shows bright streaks through the center, produced by the ridge lines. Each filter selects a blob in this spectrum, and the inverse FFT shows where in the image the selected frequencies occur. Scale 3, the lowest frequency, responds with broad blobs in the clouds and along the horizon. Scales 2 and 1 respond to increasingly thin structures along the mountain contour. Direction 4 at scale 1 picks up different segments of the contour than direction 2, because the ridges on the two sides of the summit run in different directions.

Padding matters for a second reason. The discrete Fourier transform treats the image as periodic, as if its right border continued with its left border and its bottom with its top. The product of two spectra therefore computes a circular convolution, in which a filter near the border reaches across to the opposite side. For an ordinary convolution with a

On a 400 by 600 crop of the Matterhorn photo, filtering with a 31 by 31 Gabor kernel without padding produces errors of up to 3229 in the first 30 rows and columns, more than the largest correct response in the crop (2849). Away from these borders, the result agrees with direct convolution to within
, and with padding to 430 by 630 it agrees everywhere. Zero padding creates an artificial edge at the image border; padding with a mirrored copy of the image avoids it.
